title: Elon Musk's SpaceX submits plans for $55B Terafab chip facility
content:
Elon Musk's SpaceX (SPAX.PVT) has filed plans to invest $55 billion into building a Terafab facility in Texas, which will allow the company to produce in-house chips for its AI and robotics projects.

Yahoo Finance Senior Autos Reporter Pras Subramanian dives into the details.

Video Transcript

00:00 Josh

Must SpaceX files paperwork here, build the uh Terra Fab chip plant. Initial spend of 55 billion. Maybe start here, just explain um for the audience Pras, simply what is Terrafab, right? Explain that for us. And what is Musk's sort of vision here? What's the grand strategy?

00:27 Pras

Yeah, so Musk has said for for a while now that he can't get enough, you know, high-powered chips, high-end chips to to you know, to power his his cars, Optimus robots, FSD, uh servers, you know, that that are in their in their supercomputers, things like that. So he said, you know what, I'm going to make my own. And and as we know, this is a intense and unbelievable undertaking, right? You know, this these, you know, they they measure these projects in in in in decades, right? Not just years, right? So, um the fact that he wants to do this is pretty is pretty kind of overwhelming. But basically what he wants to do is build this Terra Fab, this chip processing, chip manufacturing facility uh in Texas. And what we hear what we saw now with a with a filing is that it's going to happen in a place called Grimes County, which is near Houston. You mentioned that $55 billion spend. That's just the initial spend. It could go as high as $119 billion if all the phases are done.

01:21 Josh

What are going to be, Pras, do you think the potential sort of big hurdles for Terrafab for this Musk vision? You know, what it'd be, is it going to be money? Is it going to be talent? Is it going to be tech? Is it going to be all three?

01:42 Pras

I really think you I mean, you nailed it there. It's it's going to be all three. But I but I as someone who's not necessarily a chip expert, what I've heard though is that to make a facility like this is very difficult because you got to have good sort of um you want to be able to make enough chips that that are actually of of quality, right? You're going to go through a lot of process where you get chips that aren't ready that aren't good enough for for use, right? I think that's what that's I guess it's called, you know, the the the throughput or the output of of a of a TSMC factory or a Samsung factory. They're able to iterate and make it such that they can get a good yield, I guess, of their chips. I think that'll be the big issue, uh Josh, as they build everything out, they have the design they want, and they got to actually make these things and and they may not get the yield that they want. It's going to cost more money, more you're going to need more people, more expertise and they've also been supposedly hiring people from Taiwan uh from TSMC potentially to to come help them.

02:44 Josh

What is the timeline here, Pras? What, you know, when might might we see these chips? Is Musk saying? Is are analysts taking a stab at it?

02:55 Pras

Um, my understanding is that this is just early. I mean, look, on June 3rd, there this this a filing that said this is actually just to to get the actual abatement for the for the county for tell them to get the money uh to or to get abatement to make this thing. It's going it's going to take years. It takes years to build these facilities, not just the the actual building, but then all the equipment and get it all set up. Uh Morgan Stanley had a note out a couple of weeks ago saying that it would take you wouldn't see the first chip until mid 2028 at the earliest. So that's what we're talking about.

03:26 Josh

Musk is working with Intel on this, Pras. Explain that relationship to us.

03:34 Pras

So apparently, um Musk has said, you know, I think people have probably brought up the fact that, hey, you have no expertise in in making chips. And then we then we heard this an Intel announcement where they're going to use, I think it's called a uh the 14A is the is the is this process that that Intel hasn't even done yet for their high-end chips. I'll with Dan Howley about that. He knows more about that stuff. But but basically, uh he's acknowledging that he needs outside help. He needs, you know, Intel's America's only fabricator, right? So, it's a good interesting relationship that they're striking there. But this but this is also for a design or process that Intel itself hasn't even done yet.

04:22 Josh

Finally, Pras, you know, this is all happening of course as as SpaceX could IPO soon. You know, make a public debut. I'm just curious what you think news like this, what it kind of means for the SpaceX story? Do you think it makes it more attractive to investors? Does it make it more complicated? What do you think?

04:49 Pras

You know, I I think traditionally speaking, if before a public offering, a company probably wouldn't uh start making massive capital outlays, multi-year projects, you know, talking hundreds of billions of dollars. You neces you don't necessarily wouldn't see that. Uh SpaceX is its own thing. It's a thing that we probably are never going to see again, right? This this massive rocket launching company that started from nothing, and now people are sort of on the Musk train and they're okay. Hey, this is what SpaceX should be doing. They should be investing heavily in in R&D and capital outlays. They should be doing these things that will make this this this not just a 10X stock, but like a 100x or 200x stock, right? So I think from a enthusiasm point of view, it probably doesn't dissuade people who are originally going to buy the stock. But, you know, we we talk about these road shows, right? And if you're these banks that are looking at allocations and they're they're telling telling themselves, you know, maybe we don't want that big of an allocation. This company's just going crazy with. I mean, well, we got to see that filing, right? I'm crazy I'm curious to see what that filing says that confidence filing, talking about capital. It could be even more than what we think.

05:43 Josh

Pras, thank you, buddy. Appreciate it.

05:47 Pras

Thanks, man.

Those Arm chips are coming and you know, we're starting to see more of those. That's Nvidia has an Arm CPU. Uh Qualcomm is going further into the data center. That's an Arm CPU. So there's a lot of competition starting to bubble up between not just GPUs but CPUs as well.

title: Cerebras IPO Demand Tops $10 Billion As AI Chip Listing Heats Up
content:
This article first appeared on GuruFocus.

Cerebras Systems is drawing strong investor attention ahead of what could become the biggest US IPO so far this year, as the artificial intelligence chipmaker asks institutional buyers to state both the number of shares they want and the maximum price they are willing to pay. According to people familiar with the matter, Morgan Stanley, which is leading the offering, is seeking limit orders to help Cerebras and its underwriters better measure demand at different valuation levels. Cerebras is seeking to raise as much as $3.5 billion in an initial public offering expected to price May 13, with the shares set to trade on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the symbol CBRS. The request marks a shift from the typical IPO process, where most investors usually place market orders and accept the price set after the company reviews demand across the book.

Warning! GuruFocus has detected 7 Warning Signs with INTC. Is INTC fairly valued? Test your thesis with our free DCF calculator.

The move could possibly increase pressure on investors to bid at a higher price per share if they want to avoid losing allocations to buyers willing to pay more. That dynamic matters because the offering already appears to have momentum, with banks receiving indications of interest for more than $10 billion of shares before formal marketing began early Monday, according to people familiar with the matter. Cerebras' listing would be this year's largest US IPO so far, based on Bloomberg-compiled data, placing the company at the center of a market that has become increasingly receptive to AI-linked chip stories. Still, details of the IPO, including pricing and size, remain subject to change as deliberations continue, while representatives for Cerebras and Morgan Stanley declined to comment.

The broader backdrop could be helping the deal. Optimism around artificial intelligence has fueled a sharp move across chip stocks, with the Philadelphia Stock Exchange Semiconductor Index rising more than 40% over the past month, led by a jump in Intel (NASDAQ:INTC). For investors, Cerebras is coming to market at a moment when demand for AI infrastructure remains one of the strongest narratives in equities, and its order-book strategy may offer a closer read on how much investors are willing to pay for that exposure. Alongside Morgan Stanley, the offering is being led by Citigroup (NYSE:C), Barclays, and UBS Group (NYSE:UBS), giving Cerebras a major underwriting group as it moves toward one of the most closely watched AI IPOs of the year.
